prompt.context: Our client, OOS, is a leading manufacturer of office products in 1992, with sales of $275M in 1991. They have strong brands, invest heavily in marketing and advertising, and have grown through product line extensions and four key acquisitions. OOS is organized into 5 autonomous divisions but shares manufacturing and marketing functions. Shared costs (45% of total) are allocated on a percent-of-sales method. There are three plants running at a current capacity utilization of 50%. Analysts predict OOS is a potential acquisition target given its strong balance sheet but weakening earnings. They are publicly traded and have little long-term debt.
prompt.question: As a potential investor, how would you improve OOS's profitability?

clarifying_info.q: How has the U.S. office supplies market been trending?
clarifying_info.a: The market grew at 5% CAGR historically. In 1990 and 1991 the market declined at 5% per year.

clarifying_info.q: What is happening in the distribution channel?
clarifying_info.a: The superstore channel is becoming increasingly critical. Superstores gained 10 share points in the past 2 years, typically discount products 30% to small retailers/dealers, and are aggressively substituting private label products for traditional brand names.

clarifying_info.q: How does OOS's product line compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: OOS has a broader product line than competitors: 12,500 SKUs vs. 4,000-5,000 for competitors.

clarifying_info.q: What is OOS's most profitable product?
Are exchange rate fluctuations or import duties a factor?
clarifying_info.a: No, those are not a factor in this case.

exhibits.title: OOS Sales / Profit Trend
exhibits.shows: A chart showing OOS annual sales and profits from the early 1980s through 1991, with two separate lines tracking each metric over time.
exhibits.data: Sales of $275M in 1991; pre-tax profits of $25M in 1991; sales and profits moved together in the 1980s but profits have declined more steeply than sales in recent years.

exhibits.title: Overview of OOS Production Plants
exhibits.shows: A table or map summarizing OOS's three manufacturing plants (Chihuahua, Mexico; Michigan; New Jersey) with each plant's SKU capacity and current SKU allocation.
exhibits.data: Chihuahua plant: capacity ~12,000 SKUs, currently produces 4,500 SKUs; Michigan plant: produces 5,000 SKUs; New Jersey plant: produces 3,000 SKUs; total current SKUs: 12,500; combined capacity utilization: 50%.

exhibits.title: Plant Operating Costs
exhibits.shows: A table showing fixed costs and variable costs per SKU for each of the three plants.
exhibits.data: Chihuahua: $20M fixed + $4,000 variable cost per SKU; Michigan: $15M fixed + $7,900 variable cost per SKU; New Jersey: $18M fixed + $8,500 variable cost per SKU.

framework: 1. Examine OOS's recent financial performance to diagnose declining profitability (Exhibit 1)
2. Analyze capacity utilization and identify plant consolidation options (Exhibit 2)
3. Quantify the profitability impact of plant consolidation scenarios (Exhibit 3)

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, why have profits declined more steeply than sales?
questions.guidance: Strong answer notes two things: (1) the fixed-cost nature of the business means that as sales fall, profits fall disproportionately; (2) the growth-through-acquisitions strategy in the 1980s prevented OOS from capturing economies of scale, which explains why profitability did not grow faster than sales during the expansion years.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what are the options for plant consolidation, and which is most feasible?
questions.guidance: The Chihuahua plant alone has capacity for ~12,000 SKUs, which is close to OOS's full 12,500 SKU count. Two main options: (A) close the Chihuahua plant and consolidate all production in the two U.S. plants; (B) close both U.S. plants, discontinue ~500 SKUs, and move all production to Chihuahua. Option B is more feasible because Chihuahua has the lowest variable cost per SKU ($4,000 vs. $7,900 and $8,500), so consolidating there minimizes variable production costs despite requiring a small SKU reduction.

questions.prompt: If OOS consolidates all production to Chihuahua (closing Michigan and New Jersey), how would revenues change?
questions.guidance: Calculate revenue per SKU, then the revenue loss from eliminating 500 SKUs.

math.setup: Total sales / total SKUs = revenue per SKU; then multiply by SKUs eliminated.
steps: Revenue per SKU = $275M / 12,500 SKUs = $22,000 per SKU

questions.prompt: How would consolidating to Chihuahua change total production costs?
questions.guidance: Calculate current total costs across all three plants, then the new cost for Chihuahua running all 12,000 SKUs.

math.setup: Total cost per plant = Fixed cost + (Variable cost per SKU x SKUs produced). Sum all three for current total, then compute Chihuahua-only scenario.
math.answer: Production costs fall from $136M to $68M, a saving of $68M per year.

questions.prompt: How would this change pre-tax profits? (currently $25M/year)
questions.guidance: Combine the revenue reduction and the cost savings to compute the net profit impact.

math.setup: New profit = Current profit - revenue loss + cost savings.
math.answer: Pre-tax profits rise from $25M to $82M, more than tripling.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative issues should OOS consider when implementing plant consolidation?

categories.name: Implementation timeline
ideas: Consolidation will take significant time to plan and execute; it will not be done overnight
A phased transition plan is required

categories.name: Labor and unions
ideas: If production employees in the plants being closed are unionized, labor negotiations are required
Severance, retraining, or relocation programs may be needed

categories.name: Distribution and warehousing
ideas: Moving production to Mexico may increase transportation costs to U.S. customers
A carefully developed transition plan for distribution and warehousing is essential

categories.name: Purchasing
ideas: OOS will need to transition from smaller local purchasing departments to a strong central purchasing function

categories.name: Culture and communication
ideas: Communicating the change properly is key to ensuring employee morale does not suffer

categories.name: SKU reduction benefits
ideas: Eliminating 500 SKUs may also yield savings from reduced inventory holding costs
Fewer SKUs can simplify operations and reduce complexity

categories.name: Revenue risk
ideas: Loss of 500 SKUs could cede shelf space or customer relationships to competitors
Superstores already substituting private label; SKU reduction could accelerate share loss

recommendation: OOS should eliminate 500 SKUs and consolidate all production to the Chihuahua plant.
This raises annual pre-tax profits from $25M to $82M, more than tripling profitability, while reducing revenues only 4% (from $275M to $264M).
risks: Transportation costs from Mexico to U.S. customers may partially offset savings
SKU reduction may allow competitors or private-label products to capture lost shelf space
Union or labor relations issues at the closing U.S. plants could delay or increase costs of implementation
Currency or geopolitical risk in Mexico (though exchange rate fluctuations are flagged as out of scope for this case)
next_steps: Develop a detailed transition and implementation timeline for plant closure
Determine which 500 SKUs to eliminate based on margin and strategic importance
Negotiate with unions and develop employee transition plans for Michigan and New Jersey plants
Build a central purchasing organization to replace local plant-level procurement
Model transportation cost impact of Mexico-based production to validate the $57M net profit improvement
